claims.claim: Iliad quoted verbatim from Samuel Butler's prose translation (1898; Butler d. 1902), Gutenberg #2199; header checked (Translator: Samuel Butler).
Odyssey quoted verbatim from Butler's prose translation (1900), Gutenberg #1727; header checked (Translator: Samuel Butler). Plan's Gutenberg number confirmed from the file header.

Plato, Republic II.377d–378e, 379c–380c; III.386a–387b, 388a–388e verbatim from Jowett (1871; 3rd ed. 1888; d. 1893), Gutenberg #1497; Stephanus ranges assigned by content (Jowett's Gutenberg text has no Stephanus numbers).

Augustine, Confessions I.13, I.14, I.16 verbatim from Pusey (1838; d. 1882), Gutenberg #3296; chapters identified by opening words: I.13 'But why did I so much hate the Greek', I.14 'Why then did I hate the Greek classics', I.16 'But woe is thee, thou torrent'; the second paragraph ('For what more miserable') is the continuation of I.13. Cuts marked '…'.

claims.source: extract.py; standard Greek line numbering (Monro–Allen OCT)

claims.claim: Iliad has about 15,700 lines, Odyssey about 12,100; 24 books each.
Herodotus dates Homer and Hesiod about 400 years before his own time.
Plato calls Homer the educator of Greece (reporting the view of Homer's praisers) and speaks of 'the ancient quarrel between philosophy and poetry'; admits love of Homer from childhood.

Milman Parry's doctoral thesis, L'Épithète traditionnelle dans Homère, Paris 1928; fieldwork in Yugoslavia 1933 and 1934–35 with Albert Lord; Avdo Međedović sang/dictated The Wedding of Smailagić Meho (over 12,000 lines).
claims.source: Lord, The Singer of Tales (1960); Lord's ed. of the Wedding (1974)

claims.claim: Schliemann dug at Hisarlik from 1871 following Frank Calvert; 'Priam's treasure' belongs to Troy II (c. 2500–2300 BC); Blegen excavated 1932–38 and identified Troy VIIa (destroyed c. 1180 BC) as Homer's; Korfmann excavated 1988–2005 and argued for a large lower town; Frank Kolb criticised him (AJA 108, 2004).
claims.source: Bryce, The Trojans and Their Neighbours (2006); Kolb (2004)

claims.claim: Hittite Wilusa = Ilios, Ahhiyawa = Achaeans (widely, not universally, accepted); Alaksandu treaty with Muwatalli II, c. 1280 BC.
Ventris deciphered Linear B in 1952; the tablets include the names a-ki-re-u (Achilleus) and e-ko-to (Hektor).
claims.source: Ventris and Chadwick, Documents in Mycenaean Greek (1956)

claims.claim: Boar's-tusk helmet described at Iliad X.261–265; such helmets found in Mycenaean graves.
Peisistratean recension tradition reported by Cicero.
Aristotle praises the unity of Homer's plots.
F. A. Wolf, Prolegomena ad Homerum (1795).

Agamemnon's offer IX.121–156 (Butler's Book IX); Achilles sings klea andrōn IX.189; Agamemnon's demand that Achilles yield IX.158–161; Phoenix's 'speaker of words and doer of deeds' IX.443; Meleager and the Prayers IX.502–605; Ajax calls Achilles pitiless IX.628–632; Achilles will stay until Hector reaches the ships IX.650–655.
Kleos aphthiton (IX.413) matches Vedic śrávas ákṣitam.
claims.source: Nagy, The Best of the Achaeans (1979); M. L. West, Indo-European Poetry and Myth (2007)

claims.claim: The dipping of Achilles in the Styx first appears in Statius' Achilleid (c. AD 95), not in Homer.
Sarpedon's statement of the heroic code.
Adam Parry, 'The Language of Achilles', TAPA 87 (1956).
Redfield, Nature and Culture in the Iliad: The Tragedy of Hector (1975); Pat Barker, The Silence of the Girls (2018).
Glaucus' leaves simile VI.146–149; Glaucus and Diomedes exchange armour VI.119–236; Isaiah 40:6, 8 (WEB).
Hector stays outside out of shame XXII.99–110; Zeus pities Hector and Athena dissuades him XXII.167–185; the golden scales XXII.209–213.
Simoeisius' death IV.473–489.

Achilles sacrifices twelve Trojans, and the poet calls it evil, XXIII.175–176; Achilles drags Hector round Patroclus' tomb XXIV.14–18; Apollo's speech XXIV.39–54; Thetis brings Zeus's command XXIV.126–137; Hermes guides Priam XXIV.334–467.
androphonous ('man-slaying') is used of Achilles' hands at XVIII.317 and XXIV.479.
Simone Weil, 'L'Iliade ou le poème de la force', Cahiers du Sud, Dec 1940–Jan 1941, under the anagram Émile Novis; English tr. Mary McCarthy 1945. Weil described in our own words only; no quotation.
Jonathan Shay, Achilles in Vietnam (1994): betrayal of 'what's right' and the berserk state. Described in our own words; 'what's right' and 'berserk' are Shay's terms.
Plutarch: Alexander kept the Iliad under his pillow with a dagger.
Sophocles, Antigone (c. 441 BC), the unwritten laws.
Whitman on ring composition between Iliad I and XXIV.
claims.source: Cedric Whitman, Homer and the Heroic Tradition (1958)

claims.claim: Calypso held Odysseus seven years.
Penelope's web.
homophrosynē.
'Nobody' and the Cyclops.
Zeus on mortals' folly I.32–43; Zeus on Odysseus' wisdom I.65–67.
Massacre of the suitors; twelve maids hanged and Melanthius mutilated XXII.465–477; Athena imposes peace XXIV.528–548.
Eumaeus XIV; Euryclea and the scar XIX.386–475; Laertes XXIV; Argus XVII.290–327.
'Nostalgia' coined by Johannes Hofer, Basel 1688.
Vernant, 'The Refusal of Odysseus', in Schein (ed.), Reading the Odyssey (1996). In our own words.
Samuel Butler, The Authoress of the Odyssey (1897).
Odysseus' mother's ghost slips through his arms three times.
Xenophanes B11 (gods given human vices), B15–16 (Ethiopians, Thracians, oxen and horses), B23–26 (one god); Heraclitus B42 (Homer to be thrown out and flogged). Paraphrased, not quoted.
Plato's rules: God cause of good only 379b–c; unchanging, no disguises 381d; truthful, Agamemnon's dream 383a.
Pandarus breaks the truce at Athena's prompting.
Theagenes of Rhegium (c. 525 BC) first known allegorist; Porphyry, On the Cave of the Nymphs.
Nietzsche, 'Homer's Contest' (1872) and Genealogy of Morality, First Essay (1887); described in our own words.
Aristotle Poetics 6 (pity and fear, catharsis) and 25 (answers to Homer's critics).
Augustine born Thagaste 354, converted 386, bishop of Hippo c. 395–430, Confessions c. 397–400.
claims.source: Standard reference (Peter Brown, Augustine of Hippo)

claims.claim: The quotation in Confessions I.16 ('These were Homer's fictions…') is from Cicero.
Jerome's dream ('Ciceronianus es, non Christianus'), described in a letter of 384.
Tertullian, 'What has Athens to do with Jerusalem?'
Clement reads Odysseus at the mast as the Christian bound to the cross.
claims.source: Clement of Alexandria, Exhortation to the Greeks (Protrepticus) 12

claims.claim: Dante places Homer first of the poets in Limbo; Petrarch received a Greek Homer from Nicholas Sigeros in 1354; editio princeps Florence 1488 (Demetrius Chalcondyles).
Eustathius of Thessalonica (12th c.) wrote commentaries on both poems.
Chapman 1598–1616; Pope Iliad 1715–20, Odyssey 1725–26; Keats sonnet 1816; Tennyson 'Ulysses' 1842; Joyce Ulysses 1922; Atwood The Penelopiad 2005.
Milton prefers the 'better fortitude of patience and heroic martyrdom' to epic war.
claims.source: Paradise Lost IX.31–32 (paraphrased in the debate)

claims.claim: Jeremiah 9:23–24, 2 Corinthians 12:9–10, Philippians 2:6–8, Luke 10:20, Matthew 5:44, Genesis 50:17, 20, Isaiah 40:6, 8, 1 Corinthians 2:8 quoted from the WEB via web.py.

Paintings described only from the NGA's own descriptions: Vouet and Studio, The Muses Urania and Calliope (c. 1634, ec3850a9-…); Ingres, Ulysses (1827, f58ba808-…); Bellini and Titian, The Feast of the Gods (1514/1529, 3a640014-…); Claude Lorrain, The Judgment of Paris (1645/1646, 6f7521dc-…).
